column4: A predictor has two parts, the representation and the model.
The representation also shapes what counts as similar, since similarity depends on both the representation and the coefficient.
Activity cliffs and uninformative features, in turn, break the similar property principle.
Real assay noise is often neither independent nor identically distributed, and it need not be zero-mean.
For this reason we defined seven artificial noise conditions.
Methods for noisy labels fall into noise detection, noise mitigation and noise-robust training.
Whichever group a method belongs to, none is expected to win on every dataset.
On hERG K_i the hybrid is ahead in both halves, by less on the rare half, and on hERG blocking it is ahead on the rare half with LightGBM only.
On every small-molecule dataset the hybrid beats the best single representation with both downstream models, and it beats even the representation that was best in hindsight.
Its gain is therefore more than a reduction in width.
Since we found no setting that suits every dataset and model, the settings should be searched for each new task rather than fixed in advance.
Finally, the selected features can be read: on LogD the hybrid picks lipophilicity and basicity on every fold, from two different representations.
On the smaller sets, however, an ensemble of one model per representation often does better.
On reactions the method gains nothing on the additive split.
The hybrid can likewise take in new embeddings added to the pool.
In training, by contrast, using the importance scores again adds little on small molecules and helps on some small antibody datasets, with no condition that works everywhere.
With the setting picked again for each fold, it wins only on EGFR binding, G and SMAC colloidal stability, and loses on the other four and on Buchwald--Hartwig (Table [REF]).
The distance hybrid tracks error better for both models on QM9, Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD, and worse for both on hERG blocking.

Clustering is mixed: at every cluster count the hybrid's clusters are more coherent on nanobody thermostability and CHO polyreactivity, and less coherent on EGFR binding and SMAC colloidal stability (Table [REF]).
Prediction from nearest neighbors improves on all six, both at the setting fixed before the run and with the setting picked again.
In addition, the neighbors retrieved in the hybrid have closer labels.

The hybrid's distance does, however, track prediction error worse on hERG blocking, and except on QM9 and Buchwald--Hartwig its kept features carry no more label information than principal components of the same size.
QM9 separates the two things a gain can mean (Section [REF]).
A method that removes noise should leave QM9's computed labels alone and improve measured labels as delivered.
A method that also helps QM9 is, at least in part, a better way to train.
We apply this test to each kind of method here, before the sections that go through them one by one.
Deletion passes the test.
On QM9 with no noise added it made every model worse, in every configuration (Table [REF]).
Deleting 20\% of the molecules flagged by the forest residual does the same on QM9's labels (Table [REF]).
On SMAC colloidal stability and expression titer, the same deletion improved the labels as delivered and beat every shuffled control.
These are the clearest cases in the chapter of a method finding noise that was already in the data.
On the small-molecule labels as delivered, deletion found nothing to remove (Section [REF]).
Label smoothing, weighting and moving labels toward their neighbors pass the test only in part.
With the network they improve QM9 with no noise added (Tables [REF] and [REF], and the QM9 row of Figure [REF]).
LightGBM, which gives the same score on every fit, barely moves on QM9.
On Caco-2 and LogD as delivered, the network gains about as much as it does on QM9, so those gains are not evidence of noise.
The support vector regressor, which also gives the same score on every fit, gains almost nothing from any cleanup on these labels.
Label smoothing on hERG K_i is the exception among the small molecules.
Relative to its score, the network's first single representation gains several times what the same cleanup gives on QM9 (Table [REF]).
QM9 also shows the limit of the shuffled-score control.
With the network, label smoothing on QM9's first single representation beats all three shuffles, although there is no noise to find (Table [REF]).
The shuffles themselves move about as much as the network does between fits.
Passing the shuffled control with the network is therefore weak evidence by itself, and we read it beside QM9.
Changing the model fails the test, so its gains are better training more than noise handling.
On QM9 with no noise added, stacking the two models improves every configuration, and averaging network seeds improves most of them (Table [REF]).
On the labels as delivered of hERG K_i and LogD the same changes help by about as much.
Under injected Gaussian noise, seed averaging on hERG K_i gains more than on the labels as delivered, in every configuration (Table [REF]).
Part of its gain under damage does respond to the noise.
The twelve published methods pass the test in the other direction.
On QM9 with no noise added each one made the network worse in the first run (Table [REF]); in a second run about half beat the plain network, within the network's own spread.
Where one of them helps a measured dataset as delivered, the gain is therefore more likely noise found.
The heteroscedastic GP on G is the clearest case: it raises the best single representation's Spearman and makes QM9 worse (Table [REF]).
Noise is removed most clearly, then, where deletion or a published method helps an antibody dataset as delivered and does nothing for QM9.
On the small-molecule labels as delivered only label smoothing on hERG K_i clears the bar.
The test rests on one computed property of one dataset, on the first outer fold, and several methods have no QM9 result yet (Section [REF]).
They help QM9 with no noise added by about as much, so on these labels their gains are better training, not noise found (Section [REF]).
QM9, the one dataset with computed labels, gave the cleanest test of whether a method removes noise or trains a better model (Section [REF]).
Deletion never helped QM9's clean labels, and the published methods did not help it beyond the network's own spread.
Where they helped an antibody dataset as delivered, they found noise that was already in the data.
Label smoothing and weighting improved QM9 as well, as did changes to the model.
Their gains on measured labels as delivered are therefore largely better training, with label smoothing on hERG K_i the exception.
These gains passed random and shuffled controls on hERG, hERG K_i, Buchwald--Hartwig and three antibody datasets, though QM9 shows that the shuffled control alone is weak evidence with the network.
Which noise-handling method works best thus depends on the feature space it runs in.

Cleaning before the search and moving every label toward a Huber-fitted prediction gave large gains but have no QM9 result with no noise added, so their gains cannot yet be split into noise removed and a better model.
This chapter answers the research questions of Chapter [REF] on handling label noise in molecular data, then sets out how to choose a noise-handling method and what the thesis contributes.
Label noise corrupts the labels and leaves the features untouched, so this split is what one would expect.
Second, random forests were the most consistent model under noise.
LightGBM and XGBoost predicted well on clean labels and lost the most as noise rose, so a model's score on clean labels says little about how it holds up under noise.
Systematic noise, shared within a scaffold family or clipped at an assay limit, did the most damage.
A study that injects only Gaussian noise therefore misses it.
Chapter [REF] asked why published methods for learning with noisy labels did poorly in an earlier exploratory study, and found that those comparing molecules by a distance did worst.
Any method that relies on such a distance inherits the problem, which the adaptive hybrid representation was built to repair.
The method carried over from small molecules to antibodies, although there the gain depended on the dataset.
On antibodies and reactions, distance tracked the label better too.
However, prediction from neighbors was worse on several of these datasets, so the benefit of a hybrid has to be measured on each one.
Even the order of the methods changed between the hybrid and the single representations, so a method chosen on one representation may not be the best on another.
We recommend modeling the noise in a dataset before choosing a method.
Beyond new domains, a hybrid can be the input to the model that scores molecules for a generative model; the code exists and has not been run.
Which method handles it, however, depends on the prediction task and the data, as well as on the model and the kind of noise.
No single model or representation was best on every dataset we tested, and neither was any noise-handling method.
A dataset's noise should therefore be understood before a method is chosen.
The features matter as well: when the noise methods failed, we followed the failure down to the distance between molecules and then to the features that distance is computed over.
On small molecules it predicted better than any single representation and gave better neighbors.
It stayed ahead, moreover, through every noise treatment.
A new foundation model appears every few months in molecular and protein modeling, antibodies included.
